title: Date Arithmetic with timedelta and Time Zones
learningObjectives: Explain date arithmetic, durations and UTC offsets and its role in Python applications.

understand.concept: A timedelta represents a duration that can be added to or subtracted from dates and datetimes. Timezone-aware datetimes represent instants with an offset, while naive datetimes do not. For cross-region systems, store or exchange UTC-aware values and convert to a user's timezone for display.
understand.whyItMatters: Deadlines, booking windows and elapsed-time calculations require reliable date arithmetic. Timezone awareness prevents common errors when systems operate across regions or daylight-saving transitions.
understand.analogy: Date-time values are like entries on a calendar plus the hands on a clock; a duration measures the distance between two entries.
understand.analogyLimit: Real calendars include leap years, time zones and daylight-saving transitions that a simple wall calendar analogy does not fully model.
understand.summary: Date Arithmetic with timedelta and Time Zones teaches reliable representation and manipulation of Python date-time values.

explain.narrative:
## Add and subtract durations
Create `timedelta(days=..., hours=..., minutes=...)`, then add or subtract it from a date or datetime. Subtracting two dates or datetimes produces a timedelta.

## Understand duration values
Use `.days`, `.seconds` and `.total_seconds()` as appropriate. `total_seconds()` returns the full duration as a number of seconds, including days.

## Timezone-aware values
Use `datetime.timezone.utc` for UTC-aware values. `astimezone()` converts an aware datetime to another timezone. A fixed offset is not a full daylight-saving timezone rule; use `zoneinfo.ZoneInfo` for named regions when needed.

## Safe practices
Do not attach a timezone blindly to a value whose original timezone is unknown. Define whether incoming timestamps are UTC, local or offset-aware, and preserve that meaning through storage and comparisons.

examples.title: Add days to a date
examples.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
start = date(2026, 11, 19)
print(start + timedelta(days=10))
examples.explanation: Adding a timedelta returns a new date.

examples.title: Subtract two dates
examples.code:
from datetime import date
start = date(2026, 5, 1)
end = date(2026, 5, 12)
print((end - start).days)
examples.explanation: Subtracting dates produces a timedelta whose days attribute gives the day difference.

examples.title: Add hours to a datetime
examples.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
start = datetime(2026, 1, 1, 22, 30)
print(start + timedelta(hours=3))
examples.explanation: Duration arithmetic can cross midnight and month boundaries.

examples.title: Get total seconds from a duration
examples.code:
from datetime import timedelta
duration = timedelta(days=1, hours=2, minutes=30)
print(duration.total_seconds())
examples.explanation: total_seconds includes the complete duration, not only the seconds field.

examples.title: Create a UTC-aware datetime
examples.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
moment = datetime(2026, 11, 19, 9, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
print(moment.isoformat())
print(moment.utcoffset())
examples.explanation: UTC-aware timestamps include an explicit zero offset.
